4673.dq: Morphological words comprise one or more phonological words. In morphological words comprising a single phonological word the primary word stress falls on the last stressed syllable. If they comprise more than one phonological word, the primary word stress falls on the last stressed syllable of the first phonological word.

4673.prule: Primary word stress falls on the last stressed syllable of the first phonological word of the morphological word. The phonological word is defined morphologically: a lexical stem plus reduced-vowel prefixes, the prefix /bi/, and vowel-initial suffixes; a full-vowel prefix (other than /bi/) or a consonant-initial full-vowel suffix is its own phonological word. So prefix verbs with bi-/schwa prefixes stress the stem (/biˈprɔːljə/), while particle verbs and compounds stress the first phonological word (/ˈutˌdrIŋkə/, /ˈdIskdɔu̯k/). Position is set by morphological structure and affix identity, not by syllable count or syllable weight.

4674.prule: No word-level (lexical) stress. Prominence is assigned once per Intonational Phrase (IP): each IP has exactly one Prosodically Most Prominent Syllable (PMPS). In final-type phrases (FP; independent, incl. single declarative statements, i.e. citation forms) the PMPS is the PENULTIMATE syllable of the phrase, and the ultima undergoes post-PMPS reduction (final consonant deleted, except /m n/ which are devoiced; vowel devoiced; lowered intensity). In non-final-type phrases (NFP; dependent, followed by another IP in the same sentence) the PMPS is the ULTIMATE syllable, with overall rising pitch. The PMPS is cued primarily by duration (at least double the other syllables: non-PMPS ~150 ms, PMPS 300-400 ms), secondarily by the phrasal pitch peak; increased intensity is a frequent but unconditioned co-occurrence (fn.13). Position within the phrase, not within the word, decides prominence: the same string surfaces with penultimate prominence as an FP and ultimate prominence as an NFP (tail-head linkage, Fig. 3.12).
4674.srule: None: no word-level stress; 'every IP has one PMPS' and 'all non-PMPS syllables in an IP have roughly the same duration' (one prominence per intonational phrase, no further stresses).

4674.tone: No tone or pitch accent described. Pitch is a phrase-level, secondary cue of the PMPS: in FPs a phrasal pitch peak on the penultimate PMPS followed by a fall gives a high-low boundary tone on penult+ultima (p.96); in NFPs pitch rises throughout and the ultima carries the highest pitch (high boundary tone, p.98); longer phrases show a 'timed wave' pitch contour from intermediate phrases (p.97). Duration, not pitch, is the main indicator (p.97: 'it is duration that is the main indicator of the PMPS in Saweru, and pitch coincides with the PMPS secondarily'). 'Phrasal pitch accent' in the source means intonational peak placement, not a lexical pitch-accent system.

4678.dq: A Sechelt word may have one, two, or several syllables with strong stress: s-wák̲ats 'husband', s-wák̲áts 'have a husband', ts'ú-chis-áli 'seven people', wásíx̲-ím-mút 'making lots of noise'.
4678.dloc: Beaumont 2011, Introduction p. 1, section 1.c 'The stress-mark' (p. 16 of the 23-page 'Preliminary material' in UBC cIRcle).
4678.heavy: None in Beaumont 2011. Hill-Tout 1904 p. 61 names 'quantity accentuation' as one of two broad tendencies without defining it and says 'Both these rules are frequently disregarded'.
4678.prule: No positional rule is stated: stress is a per-word property, marked on every polysyllabic headword of the dictionary ('instructional' stress-marks), and a word may carry one, two, or several strongly stressed syllables, often consecutive, with no primary/secondary distinction drawn; stress placement distinguishes related words (s-wák̲ats 'husband' vs s-wák̲áts 'have a husband'). Hill-Tout 1904 (p. 61) likewise states that he has 'not yet satisfactorily determined... the basic principle of the accent' and gives accent-position minimal pairs (sk·ómai 'hair' vs sk·omaí 'dog'; mEtcín 'lice' vs mÉtcin 'testicles'). Beaumont 2011 p. 7 (section 4 'Word formation') adds that related words are formed 'by changing a vowel; by altering the stress; by repeating part of the basic word; by adding elements to the beginning, middle or end of the word; or by some combinations of the above', e.g. ʔílhten 'eat' vs ʔílhtín 'eating between meals', s-ʔílhten 'food' vs s-ʔílhtín 'have food' (these pairs combine a vowel change e > i with an added stress on the final syllable; the stress-only pair is s-wák̲ats / s-wák̲áts on p. 1).
4678.srule: Several co-equal stresses per word, placement given only word by word: 'A Sechelt word may have one, two, or several syllables with strong stress' (ts'ú-chis-áli 'seven people', wásíx̲-ím-mút 'making lots of noise'), 'multiple (and often consecutive) stresses'; every strongly stressed syllable carries the same mark, no primary/secondary ranking is drawn and no positional, rhythmic or weight rule for the additional stresses is stated.

4679.prule: Stress is anchored to the penultimate syllable of the STEM (stems mostly disyllabic); stated for Baria only by reference to Bare'e ('Woordvorm en klemtoon zijn als in 't Barée', p. 556; Group I rule p. 540). Suffixes other than -a and -aka do not move it ('Andere suffixen brengen den klemtoon niet van zijne plaats'), so a suffixed word is stressed on its antepenult or earlier; only -a and -aka re-place stress on the derived word's penult, and the enclitic article -e attracts stress to the syllable immediately before it (alutáe 'the wood', tadojáe 'the uvula'). Adriani's p. 563 contrast confirms the reading: re-placing stress on the new penult under suffixation is 'deze afwijking van het algemeene gebruik', confined to Tawaili, Palu and Bare'e of Tojo. The position in a polymorphemic word is therefore set by affix identity, not by syllable count; for bare disyllabic stems it is the penult.

4687.dq: Stress is non-contrastive on the phonological word level. The majority of the phonological words are pronounced with stress on the first and alternately following syllables.
4687.dloc: Sec. 5.3 'Suprasegmental Items', 5.3.1 'Phonemic status of Tone, Stress, Length, and their Interrelationships', subheading 'Stress', doc pp. 51-53 (page headers '51.', '52.', '53.'); strength chart doc p. 52; examples and 'Pitch' doc p. 53; intonation sec. 5.4 doc p. 54.
4687.heavy: A 'strength' scale, not syllable weight proper (doc p. 52 chart): consonants h, w, y, n, m (possible) weak; s mediocre; t, p, k strong; d, b, g, r strongest. Vowels (ɩ), i, ɨ weak; e, a, o, u strong (u 'except when preceded by h or w'). Combinations hu, wu, hwu, nɨ and 'other weak consonants plus weak vowels' weak; 'strong consonant + strong vowel' strong. Syllables: V weak, CV mediocre, VV, CVV, CVC, CCVC strong. Footnote: 'Further study would reveal in greater detail how much stronger the second syllable combination would need to be to take the stress'.
4687.dflt: Stress on the first syllable and alternately following syllables (1st, 3rd...).
4687.prule: Default: stress on the first syllable and on alternately following syllables (1st, 3rd...); stress is non-contrastive. Override: when the second syllable is a markedly stronger phoneme combination than the first (strength scale: consonants h/w/y/n/m weak < s < t/p/k < d/b/g/r; vowels i/ɨ weak vs e/a/o/u strong; syllables V < CV < VV/CVV/CVC/CCVC), the second syllable takes the stress in 2- and 3-syllable words ('always' in hu'ra 'fly', nɨ'duwi 'sit down', nɨ'krɨpki 'cut'); in 3-syllable words whose final syllable has a complex nucleus after two simple nuclei with the weakest first, and in 4-syllable words, stress returns to 1st and 3rd with the strongest on the 3rd ('nɨdu'kai, 'yɨkrɨp'kiyɨn). When the strength difference is small the stress often stays initial, is even, or fluctuates ('nɨdidi ~ nɨ'didi; 'hɨdi ~ 'hɨ'di ~ hɨ'di).

Shaowu has six citation tones (表7-3: 阴平21 阳平33 上声55 阴去213 阳去35 入声53) plus a neutral tone (轻声): a toneless, short syllable whose pitch is set by the preceding tone (13 after 阳去 35, otherwise low short 11 in the 1998 provincial gazetteer; high/mid/low = 5/3/1 by preceding tone class in the 1993 city gazetteer). 4696.heavy: 'Any syllable containing the sequence /V·/ is heavy; all others are light.' (p. 23) Coda consonants do not count: open vs closed is a separate parameter, and only a light OPEN syllable between two heavies loses its stress (p. 24).
4696.dflt: 'In a sequence of three or more light syllables... the penultimate syllable receives the most stress'; light-light disyllables: 'both syllables are equally stressed' (p. 23).
4696.prule: Weight-sensitive, non-distinctive stress. Heavy syllable = one containing a long vowel /V·/; heavy syllables are strongly stressed, light ones weakly, and a heavy syllable always outranks a light one. Among three or more syllables of equal weight (all light or all heavy) the penult receives the most stress; in mixed words, if the penult is light the nearest preceding heavy syllable (rightmost non-final heavy) is most strongly stressed; equal-weight disyllables have level stress; a light open syllable between two heavy syllables is unstressed.
4696.srule: Every heavy syllable (one containing a long vowel /V·/) is strongly stressed and always outranks a light syllable, whether or not it is the syllable that 'receives the most stress'; light syllables are weakly stressed; a light open syllable between two heavy syllables is unstressed; light-light and heavy-heavy disyllables carry level stress. Graded, non-contrastive degrees of stress by weight; no alternating rhythm and no 'secondary stress' so named.
4696.quote: Any syllable containing the sequence /V·/ is heavy; all others are light. A heavy syllable is strongly stressed; a light syllable is weakly stressed. While it is possible for one heavy syllable to have less stress than another, and for one light syllable to have more stress than another light syllable, it is always the case that a heavy syllable is more strongly stressed than a light one. In disyllabic sequences, either light-light or heavy-heavy, both syllables are equally stressed. 4696.tone: Alongside stress, Shasta has a two-level contrastive pitch on every syllable, which Silver calls the tonal accent: §130 (p. 25) 'The Shasta tonal system consists of two contrastive level pitches, high (/´/) and low (unmarked). Every syllable occurs with either high or low pitch'; §181 (pp. 41-42) 'There are no restrictions on vowel or tonal accent distributions. It is the case, however, that Shasta utterances, whether monosyllabic or polysyllabic, do not occur without at least one high pitch.'; fn. 2 (p. 50) 'All monosyllabic words in the corpus, except two occur with high pitch'; §170.2 (p. 40) one anomalous falling accent in /tíi/ 'tea'. Stress is a concomitant of vowel length and is not contrastive; the prepausal stress variations 'condition variations in height of tonal accent' (p. 24). Bright & Olmsted 1959 (p. 2) likewise list only a 'High pitch accent' phoneme and say nothing about stress placement.

(...) A light open syllable occurring between two heavy syllables is unstressed.

4697.tone: The source describes 'two constrastive [sic] pitch levels' L/H, transcribed on vowels and also on the first half of a geminate nasal or a preconsonantal nasal (m̀mágìc 'gum', ŋ̀gánà 'count!'); High 'does not normally appear more than once in a single word'; its position 'is not invariant in all morphosyntactic contexts' and 'is assigned according to rules which are not fully understood'; 'it is not yet clear whether this prosodic system should be analyzed as tonal or as a stress system'. Tone/stress is 'affected in the formation of the modified noun form' (gàx vs. gáxsɨ̀⁺) but 'never acts as a conditioning factor'; §3 (preprint p. 4) adds that tone/stress changes may be involved in plural suffixation. Culminative one-H-per-word with mobile placement is pitch-accent-like, but the author does not commit and no positional rule exists, hence tone or pitch accent rather than a stress verdict.

4698.heavy: Rubin 2014: a 'full vowel', i.e. 'the final vowel other than ə' (ə bears stress only when no other vowel in the word, unstressed affixes included, can). Simeone-Senelle 1997 / Johnstone 1975: the 'last long syllable' / 'pre-final long syllable'; but Johnstone 1975: 11 says that in Ś 'vowels are long in stressed open syllables and in final stressed VC syllables, but it would seem that length here is a phonetic rather than a phonological feature'. Dufour 2022: 87 makes the same point from the other side: vowel-quality distinctions are 'maximal in stressed position... minimal in post-tonic position'.
4698.dflt: Rubin 2014: 43: ə 'can bear stress if it is the only vowel in the word (e.g., yət 'camel', mən 'from'); if there is no other vowel in the word (including unstressed affixes) that can bear stress (e.g., eyáti 'my camel', with...'. the excerpt prints the stressed vowel as á, and whether that is a stressed ə surfacing as [a] (cf. Castagna 2024: 52 on stressed ə giving [ɛ] ~ [a]) cannot be read from the excerpt. Mehri-proxy formulation (Simeone-Senelle 1997): first syllable if all syllables are short.
4698.prule: A word carries a single primary stress on its rightmost full (non-ə) vowel, which is nearly always the ultimate or penultimate syllable; a penult-stressed stem plus an unstressed suffix gives antepenultimate stress (Rubin 2014: 43-44). The older formulations (Simeone-Senelle 1997 by proxy to Mehri: last long syllable, else first; Johnstone 1975: final unless a pre-final long syllable) are quantity-based, but both say Jibbali vowel length is phonetic and a product of stress, so the operative surface conditioner is vowel quality (full vs ə), not CVV/CVC quantity.
4698.srule: Stated, placement not given: a Jibbali word or stress unit 'can have several stressed syllables' (Simeone-Senelle 1997: 386, JL minṣ̌érɔ́t 'middle finger' with two acutes; Johnstone 1975: 12 'many forms having multiple stress'; Rubin 2014: 43, quoting JL p. xv 'words can have more than one prominent syllable', confirmed by recent fieldwork) beside the single primary stress; none of the works read states where the non-primary prominences fall, so no secondary-stress placement or rhythm can be given.
4698.quote: [Simeone-Senelle 1997: 386] The stress in Mehri, Hobyōt, Baṭḥari, Ḥarsūsi is on the last long syllable or on the first syllable if there are only short syllables in the stress unit.
